transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2028-06-15
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~58 minutes
Location: Zoom
Shared artifacts: Slides: https://redwood.app/decks/borealis-poc-v2.pdf, Bench plan: https://redwood.app/spreadsheets/borealis-bench.xlsx

Summary:
Quick scoping call to align on private networking topology (VPC peering vs PrivateLink), data residency/regional lock requirements, egress constraints, and the benchmark / success criteria for a POC of Redwood Private. Main asks: confirm that Redwood can run in Borealis' AWS accounts with strict egress controls, measure p99 latency and tokens-per-second on a 2048-token RLHF-ish workload, and validate KMS integration for key management.

Topics covered: network topology options, regional residency, egress policy and approval flow, workload sizing (QPS / token distribution), benchmark plan and SLOs, timelines and stakeholders.

Transcript:
[00:00] Alex Reed (AE): Hey everybody thanks for joining, um I see most of the list here. quick intros? I'll kick off - I'm Alex, AE for Redwood Inference. Maya and Jordan from our solutions team.
[00:18] Dr. Lina Ortega (CTO): Hi all, Lina here. I'll be the exec sponsor for infra and data residency.
[00:22] Samir Patel (Lead DevOps): Samir - we'll be owning the VPC and peering work on our side.
[00:25] Rachel Lee (Security PM): Rachel - security and compliance, I'll be validating KMS and audit flows.
[00:30] Alex Reed: Awesome. Maya, want to give a quick 5 minute on what Redwood Private looks like from a network perspective?
[00:36] Maya Chen (SE): Sure, um hi everyone. Redwood Private is our VPC-hosted control plane model, sorry private control plane plus customer-managed data plane inside your AWS account; we can deploy inference nodes into your VPC or into a partner-managed dedicated account and we support both V P C peering and AWS PrivateLink style endpoints. Important nuance - peering gives low latency directly between subnets but you have to manage routing/CIDR, PrivateLink gives endpoint isolation with AWS NLB/ENI and is often simpler for strict egress policies. There's also a hybrid where we run inference in a dedicated account but use interface endpoints back to your control plane, which lets you keep the control plane in your environment.
[01:12] Samir: Quick Q - what's the egress story? We cannot allow outbound connections to the public internet from the inference subnets except to a very small set of endpoints.
[01:19] Jordan Li (SE): Right, so for the POC we can lock egress to just S3 endpoints (VPC endpoints) and Redwood's control plane endpoints which we can host either in a customer VPC or in a peered dedicated account. We also support NAT-less setups - for model downloads we stream via S3 VPC endpoints or we do a bootstrap bundle during deploy.
[01:40] Rachel: And KMS? All keys must be customer-managed KMS in our account with strict key policies and no key rotation outside our control.
[01:46] Maya: We support BYOK via customer KMS key material and integration with AWS KMS. The control plane will never have access to your plaintext keys; it's integrated via Grant/ IAM roles. We'll send the KMS integration doc after this.
[01:56] Dr. Lina: Good. Success criteria - from exec perspective we need three things: 1) all PII and model artifacts must remain in eu-west-1, 2) p99 latency under 200ms for our 512 token interactive workload, and 3) clear audit logs for every request. Can you meet those?
[02:14] Maya: Short answer: yes, with caveats. Residency: we can pin nodes to eu-west-1 and we can force routing. For p99 200ms that's aggressive depends on model and batch size; if you use a 70B model quantized we usually see higher p99 than 200ms at 512 tokens unless we use aggressive batching and smaller sequence windows. For the benchmark we should lock model choice and sequence length.
[02:35] Samir: The model choice - we were thinking around 13B-70B mix, but primary workload is a customer-facing assistant that does summarization + retrieval. Average request is 350 tokens, peaks to 2048 on rare jobs. QPS during peak is ~40 requests per second sustained over 5 minutes.
[02:52] Jordan: Okay that helps. We'll size the bench to simulate 40 rps with a token distribution: 60% 300-400 tokens, 30% 512-700, 10% 1k-2k. We'll also produce tokens-per-second and tokens-per-dollar numbers.
[03:11] Alex: Can you also describe what success looks like from Redwood's side for the POC?
[03:16] Maya: For us success is: one, validate network topology with zero public egress except approved endpoints; two, confirm KMS integration and audit logs via CloudTrail/Audit; three, confirm performance targets or provide a remediation plan (e.g. model quantization, smaller sequence windows, caching prefixes); and four, show cost projections to get to production.
[03:33] Rachel: On audit logs, we need request-level traces for 90 days, and immutable logs for security review. We also need RBAC and SSO via our Okta.
[03:42] Jordan: We can integrate with SAML/Okta for RBAC and use CloudTrail logs shipped to your S3 with object lock as necessary. We'll show a sample log format in the bench results.
[03:53] Evan Torres (ML Platform): One concern - we do retrieval augmented generation with an internal vector DB, that requires inbound connectivity to our RDS/ElastiCache cluster in the same VPC. How do you handle speaking to internal services?
[04:05] Maya: Two options: run the inference pods in the same VPC/subnet as your DB, or allow PrivateLink/peered connections so the inference service can call back into your service endpoints. We generally prefer co-located deployment for lowest latency, but if isolation is required PrivateLink with interface endpoints is safer.
[04:22] Priya (SRE): If we co-locate, what about patching and maintenance windows? We need a maintenance SLA and planned windows.
[04:29] Alex: For Private customers we provide a maintenance policy and can schedule node upgrades during your maintenance window. For Dedicated capacity there's more control over updates. We'll include maintenance process in the runbook.
[04:40] Samir: Back to benchmarks - what harness do you use? We need reproducible load tests we can run inside our environment.
[04:46] Jordan: We use a harness that drives HTTP requests to the inference endpoint mimicking token streaming. For the POC we'll provide a dockerized runner you can run in your test subnet. We'll also collect p50/p90/p99, tokens/sec, error rates, and process-level metrics (GPU util, GPU mem).
[05:02] Samir: Nice. We also need to check GPU telemetry - our infra team wants visibility into kernel metrics for later tuning. Is that available?
[05:09] Maya: We can stream Prometheus metrics from the nodes to your monitoring endpoint (via a pull model inside your VPC) or push to a metrics collector in a peered monitoring account. Kernel-level hooks are available but may require additional permissions.
[05:22] Rachel: Compliance note - we run periodic third-party pen tests and need assurance that the inference nodes are hardened and patched. Also, SOC2 in the next quarter may impact timelines.
[05:33] Alex: We will provide our SOC2 summary and our hardening checklist. Also we'll work with your pen test team if needed; we can provide test harnesses and scoping.
[05:40] Dr. Lina: Timeline - we want POC completed within three weeks. Week 1: infra setup and network validation. Week 2: bench runs and initial tuning. Week 3: result review and handoff. Is that feasible?
[05:51] Maya: It's tight but doable if we get the infra details and KMS policy this week. Bench runs typically take a day per config but tuning can add several days. If the infra is ready we can run initial tests within 48 hours.
[06:04] Samir: I'll share VPC CIDRs and the list of required endpoints by end of day tomorrow.
[06:08] Alex: Great. For the bench we'll propose model permutations: 13B quantized, 33B q4, and 70B q5 or int8 if you allow larger nodes. We'll include a fallback test with caching enabled for common prefixes since you mentioned assistant flows.
[06:23] Evan: On caching - can prefix caching be pinned to region and invalidated via API? We need deterministic cache controls for compliance.
[06:30] Jordan: Yes you can control cache TTLs and invalidate via API; cache objects live in the node local KV cache and we also expose control plane endpoints (in your VPC) for cache invalidation.
[06:41] Rachel: Also request to have an audit trail for every cache invalidation event.
[06:44] Maya: We'll include that in the bench logging.
[06:47] Alex: Ok let's walk through the explicit POC plan and owners. Maya, can you summarize the steps?
[06:52] Maya: Sure. Step 0: Redwood shares pre-checklist and VPC template. Step 1: Borealis sets up VPC + endpoints + KMS roles. Step 2: Redwood deploys inference nodes into provided account/peered account. Step 3: Run benchmark harness (we propose 4 runs across model configs). Step 4: Collect metrics, analyze, propose tuning (quantize / adjust batch). Step 5: Final review and decision.
[07:12] Dr. Lina: Good. Who will be the day-to-day contact?
[07:16] Samir: That will be me.
[07:18] Alex: Noted. Samir will be day-to-day, Rachel will be security approver. We'll aim to run the first bench on 2028-06-23.
[07:26] Rachel: One last security question - do you support hardware security modules (HSM) or custom key stores? Some of our regulated workflows require HSM-backed keys.
[07:35] Jordan: We support AWS CloudHSM/KMS with external key material; for on-prem HSM we have partners but that's out of scope for this initial POC. We can include a note in the architecture doc.
[07:46] Alex: Okay, I think we've captured the core items. Any outstanding questions?
[07:50] Evan: Can Redwood show us a short example of the audit log format?
[07:53] Jordan: Yes will attach a sample log file to the bench results.
[07:57] Priya: And maintenance window process?
[07:59] Alex: We'll include that in the runbook.
[08:02] Dr. Lina: Great. Thanks all.
[08:05] Alex: We'll follow up with the runbook and bench spreadsheet. Samir, Rachel, check slack for invites to the infra channel.
[08:13] Samir: Thanks, talk soon.

End of transcript.
